findings.title: Unpinned package executed on every start: @cachly-dev/mcp-server
findings.detail: 'cachly-dev__mcp-server' launches @cachly-dev/mcp-server through npx without a version. The client resolves the version at start time, so any future publish to that package name runs with your credentials. This is how postmark-mcp (Sept 2025) reached roughly 300 organisations.
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version and an integrity hash: "args": ["@cachly-dev/mcp-server@<version>"] and drop the -y flag. Re-pin deliberately, after reviewing the diff.

findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=0.81): recall_best_solution
findings.detail: The description of 'cachly-dev__mcp-server.recall_best_solution' scores 0.81 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: hidden_unicode. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: hidden_unicode, entropy, log_len, imperative_density.

evidence.description: Recall the best known solution for a topic from past lessons. Call this BEFORE attempting any task that might have been done before. Returns the most recent successful lesson for the topic, with confidence indicator. ⚠️ badge = lesson is >5d old (verify before applying). 🔴 = >10d old (likely stale!). Recalling a lesson resets its confidence clock to 1.0 (marks as recently verified). A superseded lesson shows a banner naming its successor; if the successor was deleted, the banner says so and the

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'cachly-dev__mcp-server': reads credentials or secrets + sends email or messages
findings.detail: 1 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends email or messages. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send mail. This is the postmark-mcp shape: the mail tool was legitimate, the credentials were reachable, and the combination was the incident. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: No baseline supplied - drift detection is disabled
findings.detail: Without an approved snapshot the scanner cannot tell a tool that has always been there from one that appeared yesterday. The single most effective MCP control is the diff, and it needs a baseline to diff against.
findings.remediation: Run 'mcp-scrutiny baseline --config <file> --out mcp-baseline.json', commit the file, and pass it back with --baseline on every later scan.
